Gross Fixed Capital Formation (GFCF) and Its Revised Measurement

solution.concept_anchor: Government output valuation at cost not market price

statement_analysis.statement: In India's national accounts, the output of government services is valued at market price since the government is the largest single seller of services in the economy.
statement_analysis.reason: Government services have no market price — they are provided free or at nominal charge. National accounts value them at cost: sum of compensation of employees, intermediate consumption, and consumption of fixed capital.

statement_analysis.statement: Under the 2011-12 revised methodology, improved use of CAG audit data and state finance accounts enhanced the accuracy of government sector GDP estimation.
statement_analysis.reason: The 2011-12 revision explicitly cited better utilisation of CAG data and state government finance accounts as improvements in estimating general government output.

statement_analysis.statement: Defence capital expenditure — such as procurement of warships and combat aircraft — is classified as Gross Fixed Capital Formation in India's national accounts.
statement_analysis.reason: Capital expenditure on durable military assets (warships, aircraft, missiles with useful life > 1 year) is classified as GFCF, adding to national investment estimates.

statement_analysis.statement: Defence revenue expenditure, including salaries of military personnel and expenditure on consumables such as ammunition, is treated as intermediate consumption in India's national accounts.
statement_analysis.reason: Revenue expenditure represents current operational inputs consumed in providing defence services — these are intermediate consumption, not capital formation.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) 'All four' is the strongest distractor because Statements 2, 3, and 4 are all factually correct, and Statement 1 sounds authoritative with its 'largest single seller' framing.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Government output at market price — incorrect; no market price exists for government services; they are valued at cost.
Evaluate Statement 2: CAG data improving government sector estimation — factually cited in 2011-12 revision documentation; correct.
Evaluate Statement 3: Defence capital expenditure as GFCF — established in national accounting practice; correct.
Evaluate Statement 4: Defence revenue expenditure as intermediate consumption — correct per the revenue/capital split principle.
Three correct (2, 3, 4), one incorrect (1) — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The partial-truth trap in Statement 1 takes the true observation that 'the government is the largest seller of services' and attaches an incorrect valuation principle ('at market price'). The logical flow feels correct — large seller → market price — but the entire point of government services in national accounts is that they lack a market price. Students who apply private sector logic to government sector measurement will mark Statement 1 as correct.
solution.final_explanation:
Government sector national income measurement follows a fundamentally different logic from private sector measurement.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Government output has no observable market price. It is valued at production cost: employee compensation + intermediate consumption + depreciation of fixed assets. This is a SNA-standard approach applied globally.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Post-2011-12, improved utilisation of Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) data and state finance accounts reduced estimation errors in general government output.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Capital expenditure on durable military assets creates productive capacity lasting more than one year — classified as GFCF, boosting national investment figures.
• Statement 4 — Correct: Salaries, operational costs, ammunition — these are consumed in the year of expenditure and do not create lasting productive capacity; they are intermediate consumption.

Three statements correct — option (c).

Value Addition:
• Government services systematically appear smaller in GDP than their welfare contribution because of cost-based valuation.
• This valuation issue is an acknowledged limitation of GDP as a welfare measure.
• Transfer payments (pensions, scholarships) are NOT included in government output — they are income redistribution, not production.

FISIM (Financial Intermediation Services Indirectly Measured)

solution.concept_anchor: NIC 2008 and FISIM adoption in 2011-12 revision

statement_analysis.statement: India's 2011-12 national income revision aligned sectoral classification with NIC 2004, updating it from the earlier NIC 1987 framework.
statement_analysis.reason: The 2011-12 revision aligned with NIC 2008, not NIC 2004. NIC 2008 corresponds to the updated international industrial classification (ISIC Rev 4).

statement_analysis.statement: FISIM was included in India's national accounts for the first time during the 2011-12 revision, adding an imputed value for unpriced banking intermediation services.
statement_analysis.reason: India began explicitly calculating and including FISIM in the 2011-12 revision as mandated by SNA 2008, expanding the measured contribution of the financial services sector.

statement_analysis.statement: Under the 2011-12 revision, R&D spending was reclassified from being treated as intermediate consumption to being counted as Gross Fixed Capital Formation, which had the effect of arithmetically increasing measured GDP.
statement_analysis.reason: This reclassification per SNA 2008 means the same R&D spending now adds to capital formation rather than being deducted as a cost.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is deceptive because Statements 2 and 3 are both correct and sound comprehensive, leading students to assume Statement 1 is also correct and select an option that includes it.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: NIC 2004 adopted in 2011-12 revision — incorrect. The revision adopted NIC 2008 (aligned to ISIC Rev 4); NIC 2004 was the previous classification.
Evaluate Statement 2: FISIM first included in 2011-12 — correct; not incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3: R&D reclassification from intermediate consumption to GFCF — correct; not incorrect.
Only Statement 1 is NOT correct — select option (d): 1 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap places NIC 2004 where NIC 2008 belongs. Students who know that 'NIC' was updated as part of the 2011-12 revision but do not recall the precise edition number will accept '2004' because it sounds contemporaneous with the period of revision work. The actual edition adopted was NIC 2008, aligned to the international ISIC Revision 4 standard.
solution.final_explanation:
The 2011-12 revision involved aligning India's industrial classification with updated international standards.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The 2011-12 revision adopted NIC 2008 (National Industrial Classification 2008), corresponding to ISIC Revision 4 — not NIC 2004. NIC 2004 was the classification used in the preceding 2004-05 base year series.
• Statement 2 — Correct: FISIM was explicitly incorporated for the first time in the 2011-12 series, as SNA 2008 requires its inclusion. It is an imputed estimate of banking services not priced explicitly.
• Statement 3 — Correct: R&D expenditure reclassification from intermediate consumption (a production cost) to GFCF (an investment) raises measured GDP because the same spending now contributes positively to output rather than being treated as a cost that nets out.

Only Statement 1 is not correct — option (d).

Value Addition:
• NIC 2008 provides a unified classification framework for economic activities, enabling international comparison.
• ISIC (International Standard Industrial Classification) is maintained by the UN Statistics Division.
• The FISIM calculation requires a reference rate — typically the interbank rate — to separate intermediation service from investment income.

solution.concept_anchor: 2022-23 revision and SNA 2025 treatment of data as capital asset

statement_analysis.statement: The upcoming revision to a 2022-23 base year is expected to incorporate GST Network (GSTN) data and digital payment transaction data as new sources for improving national income estimates.
statement_analysis.reason: MoSPI's preparations for the 2022-23 revision have cited GSTN data integration and digital payment volumes as anticipated new data sources.

statement_analysis.statement: India is scheduled to adopt the chain-base linking method as part of the 2022-23 base year revision, replacing the current fixed-base approach.
statement_analysis.reason: There is no confirmed schedule for India to adopt chain-linking in the 2022-23 revision. Chain-linking remains a pending reform but has not been committed to for the upcoming revision.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is the strongest distractor because students who have read Economic Survey discussions of chain-linking as a pending reform may assume it is planned for the next revision.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: GSTN and digital payment data as new sources for 2022-23 revision — explicitly cited in preparation discussions; correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: Chain-linking adoption confirmed for 2022-23 revision — this is a scope-extension of wishful-reform discussions into a confirmed schedule; no such commitment exists; incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — select option (c): Statement 1 is correct but Statement 2 is incorrect.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap takes a genuine pending reform discussion (chain-linking in Economic Surveys) and elevates it to a 'scheduled adoption' for the 2022-23 revision. Students who have read about chain-linking as a desirable reform will conflate 'recommended reform' with 'confirmed for next revision.' The distinction between 'discussed as a future reform' and 'committed for the upcoming revision' is the precise knowledge gap this question exploits.
solution.final_explanation:
The 2022-23 base year revision is anticipated to address several structural gaps in the 2011-12 series.

• Statement 1 — Correct: GSTN data is expected to be a major new input, providing transaction-level coverage of a vastly expanded universe of registered businesses post-GST implementation in 2017. Digital payment data (UPI, NEFT volumes) may also assist consumption estimation.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Chain-linking has been recommended repeatedly in Economic Surveys as a pending statistical reform that India should adopt. However, as of current plans, the 2022-23 revision is expected to continue with a fixed-base approach. No official commitment to chain-linking adoption for this revision has been announced. Treating 'recommended reform' as 'confirmed adoption' is a classic scope-extension error.

Value Addition:
• SNA 2025 (forthcoming) may introduce treatment of data as a capital asset — relevant for the digital economy.
• GSTN data covers over 1.4 crore registered taxpayers, qualitatively different from MCA21's ~5 lakh companies.
• Chain-linking adoption would require significant institutional and data infrastructure investment beyond what the 2022-23 revision timeline allows.

solution.concept_anchor: Per capita NNI at current prices welfare limitation post-revision
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is Assertion (A) correct? Yes: Post-2011-12 revision, India's per capita income figures were revised upward, but critics questioned whether this reflected genuine welfare improvement given rising inequality and the methodology's sensitivity to formal sector data coverage.

Step 2 — Is Reason (R) correct? Yes: Per capita income uses NNI at current prices — current prices mean inflation effects are embedded; a rise in per capita NNI partly reflects price increases, not just real income growth.

Step 3 — Does R causally explain A? Yes: The fact that per capita NNI is measured at current prices means that when revised figures appear higher, part of the increase is attributable to price effects embedded in the nominal measure — this directly explains why the welfare implication of revised upward figures is questioned.
A correct + R correct + R explains A → option (a).
solution.final_explanation:
Per capita income as a welfare indicator has a specific technical limitation embedded in its definition.

• Assertion (A): Correct — When the 2011-12 revision raised GDP figures and thus NNI, per capita income figures were revised upward. However, economists questioned whether this truly indicated improved household welfare, since the revision partly reflected better measurement of corporate sector output (via MCA21) rather than income actually reaching households, and since rising inequality meant average income growth masked distributional realities.
• Reason (R): Correct — Per capita income = NNI at current prices ÷ mid-year population. The 'current prices' component means that even without any real improvement in living standards, rising prices will increase the numerator. A student comparing per capita incomes across years must use real (constant price) measures for welfare comparison, not current price NNI.
• Causal link: R correctly explains A — the use of current prices means the revised upward figure embeds price effects that do not represent welfare gains, which is precisely why welfare implications are questioned.

Option (a) is correct.

Value Addition:
• For welfare comparisons over time, per capita NNI at constant prices (real per capita income) is more appropriate.
• India publishes both nominal and real per capita NNI in National Accounts Statistics.
• Population interpolation between census years adds estimation error — the denominator is itself an approximation.

solution.concept_anchor: MCA21 introduced in 2011-12 not 2004-05 revision
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because 2004-05 was the immediately preceding revision and students may assume MCA21 — a relatively early digital government initiative — was introduced then.
elimination_logic: Recall: MCA21 was the Ministry of Corporate Affairs' e-filing system launched around 2006; its large-scale integration into national accounts occurred with the 2011-12 revision.
Eliminate option (a): 1993-94 revision predates MCA21 — impossible.
Eliminate option (b): 2004-05 revision did not integrate MCA21; it used a sample-based approach for the corporate sector.
Eliminate option (d): The upcoming 2022-23 revision is expected to integrate GSTN data, not MCA21 for the first time.
Select option (c): MCA21 integration into national accounts was a defining feature of the 2011-12 revision.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap places MCA21 integration in the 2004-05 revision (option b) or other revisions. Students who know MCA21 is a government system launched in the mid-2000s may assume it was integrated during the 2004-05 revision, which occurred in the same decade. The precise timing — integration in 2011-12, not 2004-05 — is the knowledge boundary tested.
solution.final_explanation:
MCA21 is the Ministry of Corporate Affairs' digital platform for company registration, annual filings, and financial disclosures. Its integration into national accounts represents a qualitative shift from sample-based to near-census coverage of the corporate sector.

• Option (a) 1993-94 revision: Incorrect — predates MCA21; corporate sector estimates relied on sample surveys.
• Option (b) 2004-05 revision: Incorrect — MCA21 as a platform existed but was not integrated into national accounts estimation in this revision; sample-based corporate estimates continued.
• Option (c) 2011-12 revision: Correct — the landmark integration of MCA21 data covering ~5 lakh private companies replaced the earlier sample-based approach, substantially improving corporate sector GDP measurement.
• Option (d) Upcoming 2022-23 revision: Incorrect — GSTN data (not MCA21 for the first time) is the anticipated primary new data source for the 2022-23 revision.

Value Addition:
• MCA21 covers companies registered under the Companies Act — roughly 5 lakh entities at the time of 2011-12 integration.
• This coverage expansion, not just real growth, partly explains the higher GDP figures in the revised series.
• MCA21 remains in use; the 2022-23 revision will add GSTN and digital data on top of existing MCA21 coverage.

solution.concept_anchor: NSC advisory role vs MoSPI release authority back series
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because NSC does oversee statistical standards and students may assume this oversight role includes binding release authority, paralleling bodies like CAG or CEC which are constitutional authorities.
elimination_logic: Identify the institutional principle: NSC is an advisory body; MoSPI retains final GDP release authority.
Apply to the scenario: Even if NSC's appointed committee produces figures that differ from government figures, MoSPI — not NSC — has the authority to release the final official data.
Eliminate option (a): NSC cannot compel release of its figures — it has no binding authority.
Eliminate options (c) and (d): Parliament's Standing Committee and the Finance Ministry do not have formal authority over national accounts release; select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (a) exploits the plausible authority of the NSC. Students who know NSC was created precisely to provide independent statistical oversight may conclude it has binding release authority. The critical institutional fact is that NSC is advisory only — demonstrated precisely by the 2018 back series episode where MoSPI released its own figures despite NSC's committee being unable to reconcile the data.
solution.final_explanation:
This scenario is essentially the 2018 back series controversy in a generalised form.

The institutional structure of India's statistical system places MoSPI — a government ministry — as the final authority on national income data release. The National Statistical Commission (NSC), despite its quasi-independent structure, is an advisory body without binding release authority.

• Option (a): Incorrect — NSC cannot direct MoSPI to release its figures. NSC's recommendations are advisory, not binding. The 2018 back series episode confirmed this when the government released different figures.
• Option (b): Correct — MoSPI has the final authority to release official GDP and national income data. Even when the NSC-appointed committee's figures differ, MoSPI decides what constitutes the official release.
• Option (c): Incorrect — Parliament's Standing Committee on Finance has oversight over ministries but does not control national accounts data release.
• Option (d): Incorrect — The Finance Ministry is a user of GDP data (for budget calculations) but does not have formal authority over MoSPI's statistical releases.

Value Addition:
• This institutional design creates a genuine tension between statistical independence and government accountability.
• Countries with greater statistical independence (e.g., Office for National Statistics in the UK) have the statistics office independent from the executive.
• The Rangarajan Commission (2001) recommended greater autonomy for India's statistical system — reforms remain partial.

solution.concept_anchor: GDP GVA formula and sectoral productivity analysis logic

statement_analysis.statement: A country with very high product subsidies will have GDP significantly lower than GVA at Basic Prices, because the product taxes minus subsidies term in the GDP formula becomes negative.
statement_analysis.reason: GDP = GVA at Basic Prices + Product Taxes – Product Subsidies. When subsidies outweigh product taxes, the net term is negative, making GDP < GVA at Basic Prices.

statement_analysis.statement: GVA at Basic Prices is preferred for sectoral analysis because it isolates productive performance from the distorting effects of government tax and subsidy policies on product prices.
statement_analysis.reason: Since GVA at Basic Prices excludes product taxes and subsidies, it provides a cleaner measure of how much value each sector actually created, independent of policy distortions.

statement_analysis.statement: Factor Cost and Basic Prices are equivalent measures in countries that have zero production taxes and subsidies, but differ in all other cases.
statement_analysis.reason: Factor Cost excludes ALL taxes including product taxes. Basic Prices include production taxes/subsidies but exclude product taxes/subsidies. They are equivalent only when net production taxes/subsidies = zero — but they will still differ from Market Prices if product taxes exist. The equivalence condition stated is correctly limited to production taxes, but the 'differ in all other cases' framing is imprecise.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) 'all three' is the strongest distractor because Statements 1 and 2 are clearly correct and authoritatively worded, making students accept Statement 3 without carefully tracing the equivalence condition.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Negative net product tax (subsidy dominance) → GDP < GVA at Basic Prices — follows directly from the formula; correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: GVA for sectoral analysis isolates productive performance from tax-subsidy distortions — this is the stated rationale for the 2011-12 shift; correct.

Evaluate Statement 3: Factor Cost ≈ Basic Prices only when production taxes/subsidies = zero — this is the standard definition, but Statement 3 claims this is the condition. However, Factor Cost ALSO excludes product taxes. So even if production taxes = 0, Factor Cost ≠ Basic Prices if product taxes exist. The condition stated is insufficient — Statement 3 is incorrect.
Statements 1 and 2 correct, Statement 3 incorrect — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap in Statement 3 merges 'production taxes' and the complete conditions for Factor Cost-Basic Prices equivalence. Factor Cost is the strictest measure — it excludes ALL taxes and subsidies. Basic Prices is intermediate — includes production taxes/subsidies, excludes product taxes/subsidies. Equivalence requires zero production taxes/subsidies specifically. But Statement 3 states this narrowly and students may fail to check whether the statement's condition (zero production taxes/subsidies) is sufficient. If product taxes also exist, Factor Cost ≠ Basic Prices even then. The correct equivalence condition is: Factor Cost = Basic Prices when production taxes/subsidies net to zero.
solution.final_explanation:
The three price concepts — Factor Cost, Basic Prices, and Market Prices — sit in a precise hierarchy.

• Statement 1 — Correct: GDP = GVA at Basic Prices + (Product Taxes − Product Subsidies). When subsidies exceed product taxes, the net term is negative, pulling GDP below GVA. This is economically significant in countries with large food or fuel subsidy programs.
• Statement 2 — Correct: GVA at Basic Prices strips out the product tax-subsidy policy layer, making it superior for comparing sectoral productivity across industries and over time without policy distortion effects.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Factor Cost = Basic Prices only when NET PRODUCTION TAXES equal zero. The statement conflates this with saying they are 'equivalent in all other cases' — actually, they differ whenever production taxes or subsidies exist. The broader condition requires both production AND product taxes/subsidies to be accounted for correctly in the hierarchy.

Value Addition:
• Factor Cost < Basic Prices < Market Prices (in a net positive tax environment).
• India's pre-2011-12 GDP was reported at Factor Cost; post-2011-12 at Market Prices via GVA at Basic Prices.
• The product tax-subsidy gap is the 'fiscal footprint' visible in the difference between GDP and GVA.

solution.concept_anchor: First Advance Estimate released January for Union Budget
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because it correctly identifies January as the release month for FAE but misattributes the purpose — 'basis for IMF projections' rather than 'basis for Union Budget.'
elimination_logic: Recall: FAE is released in January; it serves as the basis for Union Budget macroeconomic calculations.
Eliminate option (a): States FAE released in November — incorrect month.
Eliminate option (b): States FAE is the basis for IMF projections — incorrect purpose; IMF uses its own independent projections.
Eliminate option (c): States FAE released in March and used for Revised Estimates — March is when 2nd AE is released, and it is used in budget adjustments, not the FAE.
Select option (d): FAE released in January; used as the denominator for fiscal deficit ratio in the Union Budget — correctly matched.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap places the FAE release in November (option a) or March (option c). November is when advance estimates for some agricultural data are released; March is the 2nd Advance Estimate period. Students who imprecisely associate 'advance' with 'early in the year' may select November or confuse it with the Budget month of February. The precise timing — January FAE for Union Budget preparation — is the targeted knowledge.
solution.final_explanation:
The First Advance Estimate (FAE) occupies a specific and critical position in India's GDP estimation calendar.

• Option (a): Incorrect — FAE is released in January, not November. November advance figures relate to agricultural output forecasts, not the full FAE.
• Option (b): Incorrect — FAE serves as the basis for the Union Budget, not for IMF projections. IMF uses its own independent World Economic Outlook projections.
• Option (c): Incorrect — March is associated with the Second Advance Estimate release, not the FAE. The 2nd AE incorporates more complete industry and agricultural data than the 1st AE.
• Option (d): Correctly matched — FAE is released in January of the fiscal year and serves as the macroeconomic anchor for the Union Budget presented in February, particularly for calculating the fiscal deficit as a percentage of GDP.

Value Addition:
• Budget fiscal deficit % = (Absolute Deficit / FAE GDP) × 100 — a later upward revision to GDP mechanically reduces this ratio.
• FAE uses only 7–8 months of data; agriculture relies on Kharif estimates only.
• Large upward revisions in Final Estimates (vs FAE) are common in years of strong Rabi harvests or late industrial data.

solution.concept_anchor: Informal sector contributes 45% GDP hardest to measure

statement_analysis.statement: The informal sector contributes approximately 45% of India's GDP but presents the most significant measurement challenge due to the absence of formal financial records for most enterprises.
statement_analysis.reason: The unorganised/informal sector accounts for roughly 45% of GDP while being the hardest to measure — acknowledged as the central limitation by MoSPI and academic literature.

statement_analysis.statement: The demonetisation of 2016 resulted in an immediate and fully captured decline in informal sector output in India's official GDP estimates for 2016-17.
statement_analysis.reason: Informal sector estimation relies on extrapolation from formal sector data. The informal sector contraction during demonetisation was not directly or fully captured; GDP estimates for 2016-17 were criticised for potentially overstating growth by failing to reflect informal sector disruption.

statement_analysis.statement: Criticism of post-2011-12 national income estimates argued that informal sector growth was overstated by benchmarking it to formal sector trends, which may have moved differently from informal sector activity.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the documented methodological critique: using formal sector growth as an extrapolation proxy creates systematic overestimation when formal and informal sectors diverge.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) 'all three' is the strongest distractor because Statements 1 and 3 are both correct and Statement 2 sounds empirically plausible to students who associate demonetisation with GDP decline.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: ~45% informal GDP contribution + hardest to measure — well established; correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: Demonetisation impact on informal sector 'fully captured' in GDP — this is the scope-extension trap; official GDP did NOT fully capture informal sector contraction because methodology relies on formal sector proxies; incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3: Formal sector as proxy creating overestimation — documented critique; correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — select option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in Statement 2 uses 'immediately and fully captured' — two absolute qualifiers. Students who know demonetisation hurt the informal sector will agree with the directional claim (informal sector fell) without questioning whether official GDP data actually captured this. The entire point of the post-demonetisation GDP debate is that official methodology could NOT fully capture the informal contraction, leading to controversy about GDP estimates for 2016-17.
solution.final_explanation:
The informal sector's interaction with GDP measurement is one of the most policy-relevant debates in Indian statistics.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The informal sector (unorganised manufacturing, trade, services, agriculture) contributes ~45% of GDP and is the hardest segment to measure, relying on periodic NSSO surveys rather than continuous administrative data.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Demonetisation's impact on the informal sector was NOT fully captured in official GDP estimates. The methodology's reliance on formal sector trends as proxies meant that when the informal sector contracted sharply (cash-dependent businesses suffered disproportionately), GDP estimates did not reflect this — leading to the widely discussed 'missing GDP decline' controversy.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Post-2011-12 estimates have been criticised for structural overestimation of informal sector performance by mechanically applying formal sector growth rates to informal sector extrapolation.

Value Addition:
• India's GDP growth for 2016-17 was officially 8.2% — later revised, but critics argued even revised figures understated informal contraction.
• This measurement gap is a primary motivation for GSTN integration in the upcoming 2022-23 revision.
• NSSO surveys are periodic (not annual) — creating multi-year data gaps for informal sector benchmarking.
